questions.prompt: An LTI circuit is driven by \(\cos(\omega t)\). In sinusoidal steady state, its output is…
options: a sinusoid at frequency \(2\omega\) with the same amplitude
a sinusoid at the same frequency with exactly the same amplitude and phase
a sinusoid at the same frequency \(\omega\), with a different amplitude and phase
questions.explanation:
Sinusoids/complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: the output is the input scaled by a complex number \(H(j\omega)\), which changes only the amplitude (by |H|) and the phase (by \(\angle H\)) (reader Fig. 1.6).
LTI circuits never change the frequency, and they only leave amplitude and phase untouched if \(H=1\).

questions.prompt: What is \(d/dt\) of the complex exponential \(e^{j\omega t}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(d/dt\ e^{j\omega t}=j\omega\ e^{j\omega t}\) (reader Eq. 1.27). That is why derivatives become multiplications by \(j\omega\) and integrals become divisions by \(j\omega\).
• \(e^{j\omega t}/(j\omega)\) is the INTEGRAL.
• Dropping the j loses the 90° rotation.
• \(-j\omega\ e^{-j\omega t}\) is the derivative of \(e^{-j\omega t}\), not \(e^{j\omega t}\).

questions.prompt: A linear circuit obeys \(2\cdot dy/dt+3y=x(t)\), with \(x(t)=6\cos(1.5t)\ \mathrm{V}\ (t\) in seconds). What is the steady-state amplitude of y?
questions.explanation:
Let \(x=X\ e^{j\omega t}\) and \(y=Y\ e^{j\omega t}\). Then \(d/dt\to j\omega\): \(2j\omega Y+3Y=X\) ⇒ \(H(j\omega)=Y/X=1/(3+j2\omega)\).
At \(\omega=1.5\): \(H=1/(3+j3)\), \(|H|=1/\sqrt{9+9}=1/(3\sqrt{2})=0.2357\).
Amplitude \(=6\times 0.2357=1.414\ \mathrm{V}\) (phase −45°).
Common mistake: forgetting the 2 in \(2j\omega\) (using \(3+j\omega=3+j1.5\) gives amplitude 1.79 V).

questions.prompt: A first-order low-pass has \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\) with \(\tau=2\ \mathrm{ms}\). For a 250 Hz sinusoid, what is the phase of the output relative to the input, in degrees? (Give a negative number for a lag.)
questions.explanation:
\(\omega=2\pi\cdot 250=1570.8\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\omega\tau=1570.8\times 0.002=3.142\).
\(\angle H=-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)=-\tan^{-1}(3.142)=-72.34^{\circ}\).
Common mistake: using f instead of \(\omega\ (\omega\tau=0.5\) gives −26.6°), forgetting the \(2\pi\).

questions.prompt: A circuit obeys \(d^{2}y/dt^{2}+3\cdot dy/dt+2y=x(t)\). Using complex exponentials, which expression is \(H(j\omega)=Y/X\)?
questions.explanation:
Substitute \(x=Xe^{j\omega t}\), \(y=Ye^{j\omega t}\): \(d/dt\to j\omega\) and \(d^{2}/dt^{2}\to(j\omega)^{2}=-\omega^{2}\). Then \((-\omega^{2}+j3\omega+2)Y=X\), so \(H=1/((2-\omega^{2})+j3\omega)\).
• \((j\omega)^{2}=-\omega^{2}\), not \(+\omega^{2}\) (first wrong choice).
• The first-derivative term keeps its j (second wrong choice dropped it).
• The second derivative gives \(-\omega^{2}\), which is REAL; it is not \(-j\omega^{2}\) (third wrong choice).

questions.prompt: For a circuit made only of real-valued R, L and C elements, \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\). What is \(H(-j\omega)\) (the response to the complex exponential \(e^{-j\omega t}\))?
questions.explanation:
\(H(-\omega)\) is found by replacing \(\omega\) with \(-\omega\) everywhere: \(1/(1+j(-\omega)\tau)=1/(1-j\omega\tau)=H(j\omega)*\).
This is not an accident: for a real circuit, \(|H(-\omega)|=|H(\omega)|\) (even) and \(\angle H(-\omega)=-\angle H(\omega)\) (odd) (reader Eqs. 1.49–1.50). It is what makes the output of a real input come out real: \(H(\omega)e^{j\omega t}/2+H(-\omega)e^{-j\omega t}/2\) is a sum of conjugates.
The other choices change the magnitude's sign or keep the phase unchanged.

questions.prompt: A high-pass circuit has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega\tau/(1+j\omega\tau)\). It is driven by \(x(t)=5+2\cos(\omega t)\) volts, where \(\omega\tau=1\). Which steady-state output is correct?
questions.explanation:
Superposition: the DC term \((\omega=0)\) and the AC term are treated separately, each multiplied by H at its own frequency.
• DC: \(H(0)=0\), so the 5 V offset is completely blocked.
• AC at \(\omega\tau=1\): \(H=j/(1+j)=(1/\sqrt{2})\angle 45^{\circ}\), so the output is \(2\times 0.7071\ \cos(\omega t+45^{\circ})=1.414\cos(\omega t+45^{\circ})\).
Mistakes: scaling the DC by \(|H(j\omega)|=0.707\) (giving 3.54 V) or passing it unchanged (5 V); a high-pass leads, not lags (phase +45°, not −45°).
questions.figure_alt: Input waveform: a 2 V cosine riding on a 5 V DC level.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter with \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\) is driven by \(v_{s}(t)=10\sin(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) with \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). In sinusoidal steady state, what is the output voltage \(v_{o}\) at exactly \(t=0\)?
questions.explanation:
The filter has \(H=1/(1+j)=0.7071\angle-45^{\circ}\). A sine is just a cosine shifted by 90°, and H applies the same amplitude scaling and phase shift to it:
\(v_{o}(t)=10(0.7071)\ \sin(\omega t-45^{\circ})=7.071\ \sin(\omega t-45^{\circ})\).
At \(t=0\): \(7.071\times\sin(-45^{\circ})=7.071\times(-0.7071)=-5.0\ \mathrm{V}\).
Common mistake: answering 0 V because '\(\sin(0)=0\)'. The input is zero at \(t=0\), but the output is delayed by 45°, so it is not.
questions.figure_alt: Input sine and a smaller output sine that lags it.

questions.prompt: Preview of transfer functions. A photodiode current \(i_{\mathrm{in}}=0.1\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{mA}\) flows into a node where a 1 kΩ resistor R and a 2 µF capacitor C are in parallel to ground; the node voltage obeys \(C\cdot dv/dt+v/R=i_{\mathrm{in}}\). For \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), find the steady-state amplitude of v. (A later skill calls \(V/I\) a transimpedance.)
questions.explanation:
Let \(v=V\ e^{j\omega t}\), \(i_{\mathrm{in}}=\) I \(e^{j\omega t}\): \(d/dt\to j\omega\) gives \((j\omega C+1/R)V=\) I.
\(V/I=1/(1/R+j\omega C)=1/(0.001+j0.002)\ \Omega\), whose magnitude is \(1/\sqrt{0.001^{2}+0.002^{2}}=1/0.002236=447.2\ \Omega\) (phase −63.4°).
\(|V|=0.1\ \mathrm{mA}\times 447.2\ \Omega=44.72\ \mathrm{mV}\).
Common mistake: using R alone (100 mV), ignoring that the capacitor shunts part of the current.

questions.prompt: Preview of the frequency-domain view of systems. A lab measurement of an RC-type low-pass shows that its output lags its input by exactly 45° at \(f=2\ \mathrm{kHz}\). For \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\), the phase is \(-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)\). What is the time constant \(\tau\)?
questions.explanation:
\(-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)=-45^{\circ}\) ⇒ \(\omega\tau=\tan 45^{\circ}=1\) ⇒ \(\tau=1/\omega\).
\(\omega=2\pi\times 2000=12{,}566\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\tau=1/12{,}566=79.58\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
This 'find the corner from the 45° point' is a standard way to identify a first-order system from sinusoidal measurements. Common mistake: \(\tau=1/f=500\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (forgetting \(2\pi\)).

questions.prompt: Preview of Bode plots. A cascade of two buffered low-pass stages has \(H(j\omega)=1/[(1+j\omega/\omega_{1})(1+j\omega/\omega_{2})]\) with \(\omega_{1}=10^{3}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(\omega_{2}=10^{5}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). For the input \(2\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) at \(\omega=10^{4}\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), what is the steady-state output amplitude? (Magnitudes of a product multiply.)
questions.explanation:
\(|1+j\omega/\omega_{1}|=|1+j10|=\sqrt{101}=10.05\); \(|1+j\omega/\omega_{2}|=|1+j0.1|=\sqrt{1.01}=1.005\).
\(|H|=1/(10.05\times 1.005)=0.09901\). Amplitude \(=2\times 0.09901=0.198\ \mathrm{V}\).
Notice the first pole does almost all the work; the second pole (still ten times away) only trims about 0.5%. This is the kind of reasoning that makes Bode plots fast.
